newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Klima takes up baton as party leader.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Klima takes up baton as party leader.

text.p: Chancellor Viktor Klima formally took over from Franz Vranitzky on Wednesday as head of Austria's Social Democratic Party and vowed to continue the fight against the far right and joblessness.
Klima, 49, won 90 percent of the votes in an overwhelming show of confidence at the party's annual conference in Linz, 150 km (100 miles) west of Vienna.
"This result gives me the strength to take up the challenge, together with the Social Democratic Party, to guide Austria into the next millennium," he said.
It was clearly the end of an era as Vranitzky left the political spotlight after 11 years in power and officially handed over to Klima, the golden boy of Austrian politics.

The new party head earlier paid tribute to Vranitzky's achievements, saying his was a hard act to follow. "I can only follow in the footsteps of a Franz Vranitzky, a statesman, with your help," he told the former chancellor, a personal friend.
"Dear Franz, you have made Austria a modern country of high employment, high social standards and achieved our integration in the European Union. We will never forget it."
Vranitzky took the nation by surprise in January when he announced his resignation and nominated Klima, then the finance minister, as his successor.
However, until Wednesday he was still technically leader of the Social Democrats, who have ruled in coalition with the conservative People's Party since 1945.
Klima, in his strongest and most unequivocal language yet, ruled out any possibility of a coalition with the increasingly popular far-right Freedom Party of Joerg Haider.

"A party that is not for anything but always against something, which incites fears, creates scapegoats, plays people off against each other, which misuses the little people for its power politics and which has a sordid relationship with National Socialism -- such a party does not come into question for me as a coalition partner," he said.
The new chancellor's choice of cabinet, replacing traditional leftists in favour of centrists, had raised speculation about possible future collaboration with the far right.

Vranitzky, widely criticised for failing to take seriously the growing popularity of the far right, urged the Social Democrats in his valedictory speech to snatch back votes lost to the charismatic Haider.

The two men took over their respective parties within months of each other in 1986. While the Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low of under 30 percent in European elections last October, support for the far right soared to nearly 28 percent.
Klima reiterated his determination not to lead Austria into NATO in its current form and said any decision on relinquishing neutrality would have to be put to the nation in a referendum.

"For me neutrality combined with a real international solidarity remains the basic principle of Austrian security policy," he said. "Neutrality and membership of a military alliance are not compatible."
He also emphasised his commitment to job creation and traditional social democratic values, saying full employment remained his top priority.
